clinicalPearls: SVC syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: dusky/cyanotic head and neck with grossly elevated venous pressure but no visible pulsations should prompt the diagnosis.

Malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, metastatic tumours) accounts for most cases, but benign causes now make up at least 40% owing to widespread use of intravascular devices (central venous catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads).
Lung cancer—particularly small-cell and squamous-cell histology—causes around 85% of malignant SVCS.
In a young adult/young man with a mediastinal mass and SVCS, think lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumour.
Symptoms are characteristically worse on bending forward or lying supine; facial swelling and plethora are exacerbated when supine.
The clinical picture is milder when the obstruction is above the azygos vein.
Symptoms may actually improve over time as collateral venous circulation develops, and most patients improve partly for this reason.
Small-cell lung cancer patients with SVCS have a higher incidence of brain metastases than those without SVCS; new seizures more likely reflect brain mets than venous cerebral oedema.

Tissue diagnosis (bronchoscopy, percutaneous needle biopsy, mediastinoscopy, endobronchial/oesophageal ultrasound-guided aspiration, or even thoracotomy) can generally be obtained safely without major bleeding risk despite the venous congestion.

For a patient with no prior cancer history, a full evaluation is essential to exclude benign causes and define a specific diagnosis before directing therapy; in known cancer, treatment may begin after a thoracic CT.
harrison.pathophysiology: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late.
additionalDifferentials: Lung cancer (small-cell and squamous-cell predominate among malignant causes)
Malignant lymphoma (leading cause in young adults; Hodgkin involves mediastinum often but rarely causes SVCS)
Primary mediastinal germ cell tumour (esp. young man with mediastinal mass)
Metastatic carcinoma to mediastinal nodes (e.g., testicular, breast — small proportion)
Intravascular thrombosis (central venous catheter, pacemaker/defibrillator lead related)
Fibrosing mediastinitis (post-irradiation, histoplasmosis, or Behcet's syndrome)
infectionMimics: Fibrosing mediastinitis secondary to histoplasmosis (a post-infectious cause of SVC obstruction)
nonInfectiousMimics: Behcet's syndrome — SVCS may be its initial manifestation, from SVC inflammation with thrombosis
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph — superior mediastinal widening (most often right-sided) is the most significant finding; a normal film does not exclude SVCS if other features present
CT of the thorax — most reliable view of mediastinal anatomy; shows diminished/absent opacification of central veins with prominent collaterals; may show 'hot quadrate' hepatic sign
MRI — reported 100% sensitivity and specificity, though dyspnoeic patients may not tolerate lying supine
Pleural fluid sampling if effusion present (effusion in only ~25%, often right-sided, usually exudative, occasionally chylous)
Tissue-yielding procedures: bronchoscopy, percutaneous needle biopsy, mediastinoscopy, endobronchial/oesophageal ultrasound-guided needle aspiration
redFlags: Signs/symptoms of cerebral and/or laryngeal oedema — rare but carry a poorer prognosis and demand urgent evaluation
Upper airway/tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass — the one potentially life-threatening complication, demands emergent therapy
Cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest, especially with positional change — indicate significant airway/vascular obstruction and limited physiologic reserve
Risk of cardiac arrest or respiratory failure, particularly with sedation or general anaesthesia
Proptosis, glossal and laryngeal oedema, and obtundation indicate severe disease
Variceal (downhill oesophageal varices) bleeding as a late complication of chronic SVCS
harrison.prognosis: Clinical improvement occurs in most patients, partly attributable to the development of adequate collateral circulation. Mortality is determined by the underlying cause rather than by the caval obstruction itself. SVCS recurs in roughly 10-30% of patients. Cerebral or laryngeal oedema portends a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Do not assume SVCS is always malignant — benign device/catheter-related causes now account for at least 40% of cases.
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude SVCS when other characteristic findings are present.
Attributing seizures to venous cerebral oedema when brain metastases are the more likely cause (especially in small-cell lung cancer).
Sedatives or general anaesthesia in a patient with airway/vascular obstruction may precipitate cardiac arrest or respiratory failure.
In a patient without known cancer, omitting a full diagnostic workup risks missing benign causes and a treatable specific diagnosis.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading scale. Severity is described clinically by features such as presence of cerebral/laryngeal oedema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal oedema, obtundation, postural hypotension, and cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest with positional change, which together denote severe, potentially life-threatening disease; obstruction above the azygos vein produces a milder picture.
